sections.section_title: Dermatomyositis as an Unusual Cause of Neck Swelling
sections.description: This opening section establishes the core disease framework needed to understand the case: dermatomyositis as an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, the anti-SAE1 phenotype, and the uncommon phenomenon of inflammatory oedema or pseudoangioedema. The section should orient the reader to why this presentation is diagnostically dangerous and clinically important.
subtopics: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies: where dermatomyositis fits among polymyositis, immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, and inclusion body myositis
Core pathology of dermatomyositis: immune-mediated microangiopathy, perifascicular injury, and complement-mediated capillary damage
Typical clinical domains of dermatomyositis: skin, proximal muscle, swallowing, lung, cardiac, and systemic involvement
Classic cutaneous clues: Gottron’s papules, heliotrope rash, shawl/V-neck signs, holster sign, and periungual changes
Anti-SAE1 antibody biology: SUMO-activating enzyme, sumoylation, and the clinical phenotype associated with SAE1-positive dermatomyositis
Why oedema occurs in dermatomyositis: inflammatory soft-tissue swelling versus true histaminergic or bradykinin-mediated angioedema
How often facial or neck oedema occurs in dermatomyositis and why it is easily misclassified
Clinical significance of dysphagia and respiratory involvement in dermatomyositis
Why delayed recognition matters: risk of progression, aspiration, airway compromise, and long-term organ damage

sections.section_title: From Emergency Presentation to Differential Diagnosis
sections.description: This section follows the patient’s initial clinical course and teaches how to approach progressive neck swelling in a structured way. It should emphasize urgent bedside priorities, the early reasoning that favored Ludwig’s angina and angioedema, and the clinical cues that argued against those diagnoses.
subtopics: Initial presentation: 3 weeks of progressive neck swelling, proximal muscle weakness, mild myalgia, and subtle dysphagia-related clues
Immediate priorities in a patient with neck swelling: airway assessment, infection exclusion, and need for multidisciplinary input
Why Ludwig’s angina was considered first: anatomy, typical features, and CT findings that can overlap with inflammatory myositis
ENT evaluation and the role of flexible nasendoscopy in excluding structural upper-airway pathology
Distinguishing infectious deep neck space disease from noninfectious inflammatory swelling
How angioedema enters the differential: histamine-mediated, bradykinin-mediated, hereditary, acquired, and drug-induced forms
Clinical features that made classic angioedema unlikely in this patient: prolonged course, lack of triggers, non-tender persistent swelling, and associated muscle/skin findings
Importance of a careful skin, nailfold, and neuromuscular examination when the initial diagnosis does not fit

Constructing the broader differential: cellulitis/erysipelas, bacterial sialadenitis, DRESS, contact dermatitis, hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis, superior vena cava syndrome, myasthenia gravis, and other inflammatory myopathies
Red flags suggesting inflammatory myopathy rather than isolated head-and-neck disease

sections.description: This section explains how the diagnosis was established through staged testing and diagnostic synthesis. It should teach the reader how each investigation changed the probability of competing diagnoses and how laboratory, imaging, serologic, and biopsy findings converged on anti-SAE1 dermatomyositis.
subtopics: Creatine kinase as a pivotal early test in unexplained neck swelling with weakness or rash
Interpretation of markedly elevated CK, AST, ALT, and LDH in inflammatory myopathy and how to avoid misattributing transaminitis to primary liver disease
Normal renal function and negative urine myoglobin: what they do and do not exclude
Complement studies and C1 esterase testing in the evaluation of spontaneous angioedema
ANA positivity and the role of myositis-specific and myositis-associated autoantibodies
Diagnostic implications of a strongly positive anti-SAE1 antibody and negative Mi-2, TIF1-gamma, Jo-1, and OJ antibodies
Nailfold capillaroscopy and periungual microvascular abnormalities as subtle but high-yield clues to dermatomyositis
MRI of skeletal muscle: identifying active myositis and selecting a biopsy site
FDG-PET findings in inflammatory myopathy and its parallel use in malignancy assessment
Assessment of dysphagia: bedside suspicion, fluoroscopic swallow study, aspiration risk, and clinical consequences
Pulmonary function testing and chest CT: distinguishing extrathoracic restriction, aspiration-related changes, pulmonary nodules, and interstitial lung disease
Muscle biopsy hallmarks of dermatomyositis: perifascicular necrosis/regeneration, perimysial inflammation, and C5b-9 deposition in endomysial capillaries
Integrating all data into the final diagnosis: moderate to severe SAE1-positive dermatomyositis with inflammatory cervical oedema, dysphagia, and myositis

sections.section_title: Management of Severe Dermatomyositis with Dysphagia and Airway-Adjacent Involvement
sections.description: This section covers the therapeutic reasoning and multidisciplinary management of a severe presentation. It should explain why aggressive immunosuppression was justified, how each agent was chosen, and how complications such as aspiration and opportunistic infection risk were addressed.
subtopics: Assessing severity in dermatomyositis: airway-adjacent swelling, severe dysphagia, aspiration, muscle weakness, and pulmonary involvement
Why high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone was used first and how pulse steroids are deployed in severe inflammatory myopathy
Transition to oral prednisone and principles of tapering according to strength, CK, swallowing, and overall disease control
Rationale for intravenous immunoglobulin in dermatomyositis with dysphagia and refractory or high-risk manifestations
Role of mycophenolate mofetil as a steroid-sparing agent and reasons for selecting it in this case
Why rituximab was added and the place of B-cell-directed therapy in difficult or severe disease
Why methotrexate was avoided in the context of abnormal lung evaluation and concern about pulmonary toxicity
Alternative steroid-sparing options such as azathioprine and tacrolimus and why they were not chosen here
Supportive management of severe pharyngeal dysphagia: nasogastric feeding, aspiration precautions, and speech/swallow involvement
Monitoring treatment response: clinical examination, CK trend, swallowing function, respiratory assessment, and imaging when indicated
Immunosuppression safety workup before treatment: viral screening, TB assessment, vaccination considerations, and baseline infection risk
Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis during intensive immunosuppression and management of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole-related haemolysis
Coordination across emergency medicine, ENT, immunology/rheumatology, radiology, pathology, respiratory medicine, and allied health

sections.section_title: Outcome, Malignancy Surveillance, and Practice-Changing Lessons
sections.description: The final section uses the patient’s recovery and follow-up plan to teach prognosis, monitoring, and broader clinical implications. It should also highlight the recognized association between dermatomyositis and malignancy, especially in higher-risk phenotypes such as this one.
subtopics: Short-term response to therapy: reduction in neck swelling, recovery of hip flexor strength, and normalization of CK
Time course of organ recovery: why dysphagia may lag behind muscle enzyme improvement
Longitudinal follow-up: tapering corticosteroids, continuing IVIG and mycophenolate, and deciding when to de-escalate therapy
Interpreting follow-up pulmonary function tests and chest imaging after aspiration-related lung changes
Prognostic considerations in oedematous dermatomyositis and in SAE1-positive disease
Cancer risk in dermatomyositis: why malignancy screening is mandatory and how risk is stratified
Applying IMACS-associated cancer screening principles to this patient: dermatomyositis, dysphagia, male sex, and SAE1 positivity
Baseline and interval malignancy evaluation: CT imaging, PET, tumour markers, and planned endoscopic assessment
How to monitor for relapse: recurrent rash, weakness, dysphagia, CK rise, lung symptoms, and new constitutional symptoms
Diagnostic pearl: unexplained localized 'angioedema,' especially of the neck, should prompt inspection for periungual and cutaneous dermatomyositis signs and measurement of CK
Key take-home algorithm for clinicians: when to move from infection/angioedema pathways to inflammatory myopathy workup
